title: Spike in Cats’ indemnity bill in year of player pact
full_text:
The Geelong AFL club almost doubled its spending on insurance protecting directors from legal action in the same year a Geelong player with a history of concussions agreed to a waiver protecting the club from litigation should he take more head knocks.
The club’s audited financial report for the year to October 31, 2024, detailed that $80,319 was paid in premiums for directors and officers liability insurance, up from $47,150.
Directors’ liability insurance is typically paid by the employer, in this case the Cats, and protects individuals from penalties in the event they are sued. It is renewed annually. It cannot be gleaned from the report whether the level of coverage was increased, only that the cost of premiums surged.
“The liabilities insured include costs and expenses that may be incurred in defending civil or criminal proceedings that may be brought against directors and officers in their capacity as directors and officers of the club,” the accounts read.
The 2024 Geelong board consisted of then-president Craig Drummond, vice-president Diana Taylor (who resigned mid-year), current president Grant McCabe, Kate Spargo, James Sutherland, chief executive Steven Hocking, Barry Fagg, Lyndsay Sharp and Kate Betts.
Mr Drummond, since elevated to AFL Commission chairman, this week said “this matter was complex, sensitive and very carefully considered by the Geelong board at the time”. His career included five years running health insurer Medibank Private.
Jake Kolodjashnij has identified himself as the player.
Several board members were contacted by The Australian for comment surrounding the situation and none replied, bar Mr Fagg, who referred The Australian to the CEO’s office.
CEO Mr Hocking has said “the letter went further than intended”, with reference to the secret waiver.
Reports have exposed how the Geelong player signed a letter so that he could continue to play, acknowledging the risks to his health of further concussions and waived his legal rights against the club. The letter was signed without the knowledge of the AFL or the AFL Players Association and has been widely criticised by experts and player advocates as a failure to protect the individual and of proper governance.
The AFL has decided it will not sanction the Cats. Geelong has since scrapped the secret deal with the player.
The board’s corporate governance committee in 2024 consisted of Mr Drummond, Ms Taylor (who exited mid-year), Ms Spargo and Mr Hocking.
All four attended every committee meeting they were available for, except for Mr Hocking who missed one. Three committee meetings were held in 2024. The AFL has elevated concussions as a critical issue, which has included rule changes all the way down to grassroots level. The AFL is also currently facing a massive class action – led by former Geelong player Max Rooke – consisting of more than 100 past players, which is set to go to trial in 2027. The action alleges the league failed to take appropriate action on concussions.
